transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what's been bothering you or what brings you in today?

Yeah, um… I’m here because things at work have gotten strange since I got that county safety award. I’m a transportation inspector, so reports matter, you know, every word, every number. And ever since then, certain people have been… twisting what I write in my inspection reports, acting like there are “questions” about budgets or procedures, but the way they ask it, it’s like they’re trying to make me look crooked.

My supervisor keeps saying it’s just normal review, normal oversight, all that, but I can tell it’s not just that. It feels coordinated. Like they’re setting up a paper trail to discredit me. And I wouldn’t even care about the award, honestly—my mom made a bigger deal about it than I did—but after that, the tone changed. The questions got pointed. People started looking at me different. That’s what’s been bothering me.
How long has this feeling that colleagues are coordinating against you been going on—days, weeks, or longer?

Longer than weeks, yeah. It’s been about a year now, since I got recognized for that county safety initiative. I remember because everybody was being all polite at first, like “congratulations,” and my mom wanted to put the certificate up—she’s always been like that with stuff from school too—but after that, things at work just… shifted. So, yeah, about a year.
Have you ever heard voices, sounds, or seen things that other people around you didn't seem to hear or see?

I mean… not like voices talking to me, no. I don’t think so. Sometimes at work you hear things in the hallway or the copier room and you can’t tell who said what, but that place echoes weird, and people are always stepping out when you turn the corner.

Seeing things, no, not really. I mean, unless you count noticing stuff other people don’t pay attention to, like when files are moved or someone changes the wording in a report. But that’s not like… seeing things that aren’t there. So, no, I haven’t really noticed that.

Outside of work, do you find yourself distrustful or suspicious of people close to you, like family or friends, or does this feeling really stay focused on your coworkers and this situation at your job?

It’s mostly work. I mean, my mom worries about me, but she’s not part of it or anything. Friends… I don’t really bring it up much because people don’t understand how inspection reports work.

But at work, that’s where it is. Ever since that county safety award, certain people started twisting what I put in the reports, then asking these pointed budget questions like I’m hiding something or trying to make me look crooked. And my supervisor keeps saying, “That’s just normal review,” but it doesn’t feel normal when it’s the same people and the same kind of wording every time. It feels coordinated, like they’re building something to discredit me.

Aside from these concerns at work, how would you say your day-to-day functioning has been—are you still keeping up with your usual responsibilities, self-care, and relationships the way you did before this started?

I mean, day to day I’m still doing what I’m supposed to do. I get to work on time, I finish my inspections, I keep myself cleaned up, laundry, shaving, all that. I still go to church too—my mom would notice quick if I stopped, and honestly I like the routine.

It’s not like I’m just sitting around doing nothing. The trouble is more when somebody starts bringing up those reports again, or asking about my spending like there’s something suspicious there. That’s when everything gets… harder to let go of. But regular responsibilities, yeah, I’m keeping up.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a fixed, non-bizarre persecutory delusion (belief that coworkers are coordinating to discredit him via manipulated reports and pointed questioning) that has persisted for about one year. There are no hallucinations, no disorganized speech or behavior, and no evidence of a mood episode. Functioning is largely preserved—he maintains work performance, self-care, and social/religious routines—except for distress triggered specifically by report-related interactions. The delusion is circumscribed to the workplace situation rather than pervasive across all relationships, and there is no broader psychotic symptom cluster (no negative symptoms, no thought disorder), which argues against schizophrenia. The absence of any reported mood symptoms argues against a schizoaffective or mood-related psychotic disorder. This clinical picture—an isolated, well-systematized delusional belief with relatively preserved functioning and absence of other psychotic or mood symptoms for greater than one month—is most consistent with Delusional Disorder (F22).
